documentation.range: This species is widespread throughout much of Southeast Asia from the Nicobar Islands (Whitaker and Captain 2004) through Bangladesh (Chittagong), Myanmar, Thailand, Lao PDR, Cambodia, Viet Nam, Malaysia and Singapore, east through Indonesia and the Indo-Australian Archipelago (Sumatra, the Mentawai Islands, the Natuna Islands, Borneo, Sulawesi, Java, Lombok, Sumbawa, Sumba, Flores, Maluku, Tanimbar Islands) and the Philippines (Basilan, Bohol, Cebu, Leyte, Luzon, Mindanao, Mindoro, Negros, Palawan, Panay, Polillo, Samar, Tawi-Tawi). A record from mainland India (Mukherjee et al. 2012) might represent a vagrant from Bangladesh or Myanmar, and no evidence of a viable natural population has been reported from mainland India (M. Auliya pers. comm. 2018). Historical records exist for several islands in eastern Indonesia, including Timor, Romang and Leti, but the snake has not been found in recent surveys of East Timor (Kaiser et al. 2011). It has a northern range limit in central Viet Nam and Lao PDR, and is absent from northern Thailand and northern Myanmar, but the precise northern limit of its distribution is in need of clarification (M. Auliya and H. Jenkins pers. comm. September 2011). It occurs from sea level, and in the Philippines it has a maximum recorded elevation range of 1,000 km2.
documentation.population: This snake's population status, and the availability of population data, greatly vary across the species' large geographic range. The snake remains abundant in Thailand, where it can often be found in people's houses during the rainy season (T. Chan-ard pers. comm. August 2011). In the Philippines this is a widespread and common species, even in residential areas. The Philippine subpopulation is believed to be stable, or possibly increasing. Zug et al. (2011) stated that pythons are rare in Myanmar. In Cambodia this species is becoming noticeably rarer, and populations may have declined by 30-50% over ten years based on informal estimates (T. Neang pers. comm. August 2011). It is very rarely found in Viet Nam in the wild (Q.T. Nguyen pers. comm. August 2011) but has been found to be common in good forest in southern Viet Nam (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018). It is thought likely that it remains common in southern parts of this country where suitable habitat remains, including protected areas (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018). It is probably also declining in Laos. The rate of population decline in Vietnam has been estimated at greater than 80% over ten years (Dang et al. 2007). Declines throughout Indochina are likely to have been driven primarily by land conversion to structurally impoverished areas including agricultural land (e.g. rice paddies), although harvesting may represent a secondary impact (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018). It is still relatively abundant in surveyed areas of Kalimantan, but there has been no comprehensive study of the species' status across Kalimantan as a whole (M. Auliya pers. comm. 2018). Subpopulations in Malaysia and Indonesia appear to be stable despite intensive exploitation (Natusch et al. 2016a). The snake remains common in Singapore despite intensive urbanization, where dense, well-structured secondary habitat with a high density of prey remains in urban areas (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018) and harvest of this species is prohibited (M. Auliya pers. comm. 2018). In Sarawak and Sabah, the species is common in residential as well as natural areas, despite some exploitation for food, and there is no reported evidence of decline (I. Das pers. comm. September 2011). Declines driven by habitat clearance and exploitation may be offset to at least some degree by the expansion of oil palm plantations, as the snake has been reported to remain common in these habitats (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018).
documentation.habitats:
The species occurs in rainforest, woodland and adjacent grassland areas. It is also associated with rivers and is often found near or in streams and lakes. Its habitat tolerances appear to vary across its range; it has been described as occurring in sewers in Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysian Borneo (L. Grismer, H. Jenkins and I. Das pers. comm. September 2011), but only from pristine forest in Myanmar (G. Wogan pers. comm. September 2011). This species is an excellent swimmer; it has even been reported far out at sea and has consequently colonized many small islands within its range. This was among the first species to colonize the recently-emerged island of Krakatau. The species is tolerant of highly modified habitat, and occurs in urban areas in some parts of its range.

There are differences in timing of reproduction between subpopulations in northern and southern Sumatra (Shine et al. 1999). Females are larger than males, produce clutches containing an average of 24.2 eggs, and reproduce only once every two to four years (Shine et al. 1999). Fecundity also varies longitudinally, making it difficult to extrapolate figures obtained in one study to the remainder of this snake's wide range (M. Auliya pers. comm. 2011). Smaller individuals feed primarily on human commensal rodents and are abundant in human-modified habitats, including oil palm plantations (Nossal et al. 2016, Natusch et al. 2016a). Larger animals, greater than around 4 metres in length, are less well-suited to these habitats, as they require vegetated understoreys and prey on larger animals which are not associated with modified habitats (Shine et al. 1999, Natusch et al. 2016a).
documentation.threats:
Being the world's longest snake, the species is often persecuted out of fear. The species is hunted primarily for skins, but also for food, traditional medicine and pets in most of its range. These snakes are hunted for meat for domestic markets, however, they are exported internationally as demand requires (Natusch et al. 2016b). The commercial skin trade is unlikely to result in the extirpation of this species from Indonesia (Shine et al. 1999), however, a detrimental impact on local subpopulations cannot be ruled out (M. Auliya pers. comm. 2018). Data collected over a 20-year period from heavily harvested sites (involving more than 4,000 snakes) in northern and southern Sumatra found no evidence that harvesting had negatively impacted the species during that period (Natusch et al. 2016a), however, harvesting is likely to reduce the number of animals reaching truly giant sizes (6 m length or greater) as these animals are more conspicuous to hunters (Auliya 2006, Natusch 2016a,b). Exports of this species from Indonesia increased by 400% between 1999 and 2008 based on CITES figures (Luiselli et al. 2012). Although the species is highly tolerant of habitat degradation as long as suitable habitat structure remains, disturbed areas around villages render this large snake more vulnerable to hunting pressures for trade and exploitation (Q.T. Nguyen and T. Neang pers. comm. August 2011), and human population growth increases the exposure of large pythons to persecution.

This species may be able to resist intensive commercial exploitation because it has a life-history involving rapid growth, early maturation, high reproductive output (infrequent production of large clutches of large eggs), and the ability to tolerate human-modified habitats (Shine et al. 1999). Nevertheless, while this species is not thought at risk of global extinction through either hunting or habitat loss, overexploitation coupled with extensive habitat loss particularly in Indochina driven by agricultural conversion may lead to the loss of regional subpopulations, and may negatively impact subpopulations throughout the snake's range (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018). Pressures from exploitation are likely to be increasing in lowland areas of central and southern Viet Nam where human population densities are increasing, and the species may be increasingly reliant on less accessible refugia in the highlands (M. Auliya pers. comm. 2018). It remains challenging to substantiate reports of detrimental impacts from harvesting on either the status or the demographics of wild python subpopulations and it is possible that this species' distribution is more fragmentary than presently understood, especially in the core harvest areas of Indonesia and Peninsular Malaysia (M. Auliya pers. comm. 2018).
documentation.measures: This species has been recorded from many protected areas throughout its range, including multiple national parks. In some parts of its range such as Lao PDR, Viet Nam, and Cambodia, it is illegal to collect the species from the wild (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018), and ensuring these regulations are enforced is warranted in areas where declines have been reported. In Viet Nam this species has been listed as Critically Endangered in the national Red Data Book (Dang et al. 2007). It is listed on CITES Appendix II (as Python reticulatus). It is a protected species in every Southeast Asian range state except Indonesia, although in some states (e.g. Malaysia) this protection may permit hunting with a permit (D. Natusch pers. comm. 2018). On the recommendation of the CITES Animals Committee, in 2011 this species was included in the next phase of the Review of Significant Trade; the result of that review was that this species' survival in the wild was not threatened by trade in any range state.
documentation.use_trade: This species is heavily hunted in some parts of its range. Approximately 180,000 specimens are harvested annually from Indonesia each year, with most taken from Sumatra and Kalimantan (Natusch et al. 2016b). In 2017, there was a legal export quota from this country of 2,970 individuals for the international pet trade, and 159,030 for the skin trade (CITES 2017). There is, however, evidence that Indonesian harvest quotas are exceeded, resulting in a greater (but unknown) number of snakes being harvested than quotas allow. Peninsular Malaysia has an annual export quota of 155,000 skins (CITES 2018. In 2016 more than 340,000 skins of wild individuals were reported as legal exports, mainly from Indonesia and Malaysia (CITES 2017). These skins typically enter trade via neighbouring countries (Natusch et al. 2016b). The meat is consumed in rural areas in much of its range, and there is commercial demand for food, traditional medicine, and skin. In the past, the species was heavily hunted and traded in Lao PDR, Viet Nam, and Cambodia, where it is mainly hunted for its skin, for medicine and for the pet trade, and rarely for food (T. Neang pers. comm. 2011). In 2007 Viet Nam exported skins from more than 40,000 pythons reported as captive-bred to the European Union (CITES 2011). This figure likely includes pythons imported to Viet Nam from Cambodia and Lao PDR (B. Stuart pers. comm. September 2011). Captive breeding facilities for this species have been established (Natusch and Lyons 2014). Recently, a market for low-quality skins has emerged in China.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern globally, in view of its wide distribution, adaptability and abundance even in some areas where it is subject to heavy exploitation. Population declines resulting from a combination of habitat loss and overexploitation justify treating this species as locally threatened in parts of Viet Nam, Lao PDR and Cambodia.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
This species has been long known as Python reticulatus, and is still retained under this name in CITES legislation, but a combined morphological and molecular analysis by Rawlings et al. (2008) found that it belonged to a distinct lineage along with Python timorensis. Rawlings et al. (2008) accepted the name Broghammerus Hoser, 2004 for this clade, however, it was subsequently argued that this name may not have been validly published (Kaiser et al. 2013). Citing both this concern and the caution that broader genetic sampling is required to confirm the validity of the Python reticulatus-timorensis clade (Zug et al. 2011), O'Shea et al. (2013) reverted to the use of Python for this species. Reynolds et al. (2014) subsequently reported additional molecular support for a P. reticulatus-timorensis clade and coined the replacement name Malayopython.

This species exhibits considerable geographic variation across its range, and three subspecies - P. r. reticulatus, P. r. jampeanus and P. r. saputrai - are recognized (Auliya et al. 2002). The Philippine populations belong to the nominate form; however, the taxonomy of island forms of P. reticulatus, including those from the Philippines and eastern Indonesia, is unstudied and requires clarification (M. Auliya pers. comm. September 2011).
